consensus_summary: The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or salvation/gospel/Christ) as a treasure of supreme worth for which everything should be surrendered, based on Matthew 13:45-46, with secondary associations as sacred/holy truth (Matthew 7:6) and the gates of New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:21); common alternatives include the reverse (Christ as merchant, pearl as Church/believer) and negative luxury/vanity.
book_summary: The pearl is the one complete light—the full moon (keseh, fulness) of the night sky, governor of appointed times—while wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls (via KJV rubies/peninim); this is the one-pearl gates of the city as the merchant’s entry at the King’s gate.
consensus_core_identification: Kingdom of Heaven / supreme spiritual treasure (salvation, Christ, or gospel)
book_core_identification: the full moon as the night sky’s one pearl / complete light
boundary_disagreement: Book centers calendrical lunar symbolism (full moon, appointed times, keseh) and elevates wisdom/bride above pearls while re-reading the merchant and one-pearl gates as lunar entry; consensus never contemplates lunar or calendrical cases at all.
material_contradiction: None explicit; book separately notes the common kingdom/church view without denying it, but supplies an entirely different primary identification.
rationale: Consensus core (kingdom/spiritual treasure from Matt 13, plus listed alternatives) contains no lunar, calendrical, or full-moon identification. Book’s core is precisely that identification (full moon via peninim/keseh links). Absence of any covering consensus referent makes the relation novel rather than a refinement, broadening, or contradiction of a shared core. Citations supply isolated components (pearl value, moon for seasons, pearl gates) but not the identification itself.
strongest_objection: Standard NT symbolism from the Pearl of Great Price parable is set aside for an unattested lunar equation that depends on Strong’s numbers, letter associations under ‘throne/time,’ and intertextual moon-season links nowhere present in ordinary pearl symbolism.
